Abstract We describe the successful anesthetic management of a patient with stiff-person syndrome
(SPS) undergoing a right inguinal hernia repair, using a somatic paravertebral block supplemented
with conscious sedation. We also present the implications of general anesthesia in patients with SPS.
The use of regional anesthetic techniques in patients with SPS has the advantage of avoiding exposure
to muscle relaxants. The use of general anesthesia in patients with SPS carries the risk of postoperative
hypotonia due to enhancement of c-aminobutyric acid action on synaptic transmission by drugs that
have a c-aminobutyric acid agonistic action.

Case report
A 65-year-old man was scheduled for elective repair of a
large right indirect inguinal hernia. His past medical history
included diabetes mellitus, hypertension, depression, and
SPS. Past surgical history was remarkable for an uneventful

repair of a left inguinal hernia in 1965 and placement of an
intrathecal baclofen pump 9 months before this presentation.
His laboratory workup detected the presence of anti-
bodies to GAD enzyme and elevated levels of IgA and
thyroglobulin antibodies. Electromyogram findings ruled
out evidence of diffuse motor axon loss disorder. However,
there was nonspecific abnormal activation of the motor unit,
and failure of relaxation of the proximal muscle group of
both lower extremities and the right upper extremity. These
findings suggested a central disorder of the motor control
unit. Current medications included insulin, enalapril, gaba-
pentin, esomeprazole, venlafaxine, and baclofen through an
intrathecal pump. The patient was also receiving intrave-
nous immunoglobulins every 2 weeks to neutralize circu-
lating antibodies and downregulate the pro-inflammatory
cytokines [2]. He received his last dose 4 days before the
scheduled surgery date.
After discussing the risks and benefits of the different
anesthetic techniques, a right somatic paravertebral block at
T12 and L1 was selected. On arrival to the operating room,
standard ASA monitors were applied. The block was
performed in the sitting position using 5 mL of 0.5%
bupivacaine at each level. Supplemental sedation with
intravenous midazolam 1 mg, fentanyl 50 lg, and a
propofol infusion at 25 to 35 lg/kg per minute was
administered. Oxygen was supplied at 2 L/min via a nasal
cannula. Vital signs were stable throughout his surgery and
in the postoperative period. The patient reported improve-
ment of his spasticity symptoms during the procedure and
for 1 hour into the postoperative period. In the Post
Anesthesia Care Unit, he complained of nausea, which
was treated with 4 mg of intravenous ondansetron.
